g.text: 'Reservation' and 'inventory' are two nouns and one invariant
So the seam is drawn where the transaction boundary is - and the transaction boundary is drawn by the correctness requirement.
Split on genuine boundaries - change cadence, data shape, ownership
client
API gateway
auth, rate limiting, and the
split between public and
admin APIs - admin is
reachable only from the
internal network
hotel service
rate service
payment service
admin service
hotel and room-type detail: near-static, cached with a long TTL, and the highest-volume read path
per-date pricing. Its data changes daily and is owned by a DIFFERENT TEAM (revenue management)
with its own tooling and approval flow - an ownership difference that is a stronger argument for
the boundary than any technical one
wraps an external PSP: hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, and it can time out
staff tooling for hotels, rooms and rates; behind the internal gateway
Those are real differences in change cadence, data shape and ownership. The general principle, stated concretely: SPLIT WHEN
THE REASONS TO CHANGE DIFFER, NOT WHEN THE NOUNS DIFFER.
The decomposition a textbook would do - and why it is exactly wrong here
CHOSEN
reservation service
reservations AND inventory
ONE relational database
primary + replicas, ACID
One BEGIN ... COMMIT gives the double-booking guarantee for free:
no protocol, no coordinator, no compensation logic, and no window
of inconsistency.
REJECTED an inventory service and a reservation service
reservation service
database A
inventory service
database B
2PC, or a saga
Creating a reservation and decrementing inventory MUST BE ATOMIC. Split across two services with two databases, there is no
transaction that covers both - so you need 2PC (blocking, lock-holding) or a saga with compensation (eventually consistent,
meaning a window in which inventory says a room is free and a reservation for it already exists). BOTH TRADE CORRECTNESS FOR A
DISTRIBUTION YOU DO NOT NEED AT 3 RESERVATIONS/SEC.
When WOULD you split them? If inventory reads became hot enough to need independent scaling - the Booking.com-scale scenario.
Even then the better first move is a read replica or a cache, not a service boundary, because the WRITE path is what needs the
transaction and the write path is tiny.
The reservation path - 3/sec, and the only path that matters
BEGIN TRANSACTION <- the atomicity boundary
1. INSERT INTO reservation (reservation_id, ..., status='pending')
-> UNIQUE(reservation_id) violation => this is a REPLAY:
roll back and return the ORIGINAL reservation
2. UPDATE room_type_inventory
SET total_reserved = total_reserved + :n
WHERE hotel_id = ? AND room_type_id = ?
AND date >= ? AND date < ?
AND total_reserved + :n <= total_inventory * 1.10
-> affected rows < nights requested => ROLLBACK, return 409
COMMIT
3. call the payment service <- OUTSIDE the transaction
success -> UPDATE reservation SET status='confirmed'
failure -> status='payment_failed', and release the inventory
4. publish ReservationConfirmed -> notifications, CDC to the cache
Step 3 being outside the transaction is the single most important structural
decision on this path. A payment provider call takes hundreds of milliseconds
to seconds and can time out. Inside the transaction, the inventory row lock
would be held for that entire duration - serializing every other booking for
that hotel and room type behind one slow payment. At peak season with genuine
contention on a popular hotel, that turns a 3/sec system into an unusable one.
The cost is that a PENDING state now exists and must be reconciled. A crash
between commit and payment leaves inventory decremented for a reservation that
was never paid - so a sweeper releases pending reservations older than a
timeout. That is the saga trade: accept a transient inconsistency and a
compensating action, in exchange for not holding a lock across a call you do
not control.
And that sweeper is the design's most important background job. Pending
reservations HOLD INVENTORY, so a sweeper that fails silently means
availability slowly leaking away for no reason - a bug that presents as 'the
hotel looks full but isn't', with nothing in the logs. It must be monitored on
INVENTORY HELD BY PENDING ROWS, not merely on its own completion.
The other three paths - each with one idea in it
availability check ~300/sec, from a READ REPLICA
Deliberately from a replica. Availability shown to a browsing user is
allowed to be slightly stale, because the authoritative check happens
AGAIN inside the booking transaction. DISPLAYING availability and
GUARANTEEING availability are two different operations, and conflating
them would push all read traffic onto the primary for no benefit.
The cost is that a user can see '1 room left' and then lose the race -
which is exactly what the 409 is for.
cancellation guarded, therefore idempotent
UPDATE reservation SET status='cancelled'
WHERE reservation_id=? AND status='confirmed'
-> 0 rows => already cancelled or never confirmed
UPDATE room_type_inventory SET total_reserved = ... - :n
The AND status='confirmed' guard is what makes cancellation
idempotent: a double-click releases inventory once, not twice.
Without it, two cancellations decrement inventory twice and
silently manufacture availability - a bug that manifests as
OVERSELLING WITH NO OVERSELL IN THE LOGS.
horizon extension a nightly cron
The booking horizon is finite, so rows are pre-created
and the far edge is extended daily: for each (hotel,
room_type), INSERT a row for today + 2 years.
A booking beyond the horizon returns 422 rather than
silently creating rows - because an inventory row
implicitly asserts a total_inventory, and inventing one
for a date nobody has planned for is worse than
refusing.
Low throughput, high contention on a few keys - the opposite of every other design in this guide
Aggregate load is trivial: 3 writes/sec, 3,000 reads/sec. The genuine peak is CONTENTION, NOT VOLUME - a popular resort during
a holiday week means many users converging on the SAME INVENTORY ROWS. Backpressure therefore appears on one contended row's
lock queue, and no amount of sharding helps, because the contention is on a SINGLE LOGICAL KEY.
mitigation 1 shorten the transaction to the absolute minimum
which is exactly why payment is outside it: the lock is held for the duration of one UPDATE - microseconds.
mitigation 2 split a room type's inventory into N sub-counters, summed on read
the sharded-counter trick, as used for hot wallet accounts. Costs a scatter-read for availability and needs rebalancing so one
sub-counter does not run dry while others have space. AT THIS VOLUME IT IS UNNECESSARY - and naming it as available-if-needed
is better than building it.
What gets shed under overload, in order
1 search and browse served from a longer-TTL cache: staler data, no extra database load
2 availability checks rate-limited per user. Somebody refreshing a sold-out hotel every second is pure load.
3 new reservations 503 with Retry-After - safe, because the client's reservation_id makes the retry free
4 NEVER shed cancellations refusing a cancellation holds inventory hostage and creates a support case AND a lost sale.
Same inversion the stock exchange makes about order cancels: under stress, letting people
WITHDRAW matters more than letting them commit.
5 NEVER shed confirming a paid reservation the money has already moved.
Degradation - including the one hard outage the design deliberately accepts
a read replica fails
availability reads shift to the remaining replicas or the primary
at 300/sec the primary absorbs it
the rate service fails
hotel pages render without prices, and BOOKING IS BLOCKED
you cannot charge an unknown amount. Browsing survives; converting does not.
the payment service fails
reservations commit as pending with inventory held
confirmation completes asynchronously - genuinely graceful
the PRIMARY database fails
BOOKING STOPS ENTIRELY; replicas serve browsing and availability
the one hard outage, and the accepted cost of choosing a single ACID primary
Redis fails
cache misses fall through to the replicas
at this volume, invisible
The load-test target is the whole point: drive 1,000 concurrent booking attempts at a room type with EXACTLY ONE ROOM LEFT and
assert that exactly one succeeds and 999 receive 409 - no oversell, no deadlock, no lost update. Separately, submit the same
reservation_id 100 times concurrently and assert exactly one reservation exists. The correctness assertions ARE the test;
throughput is incidental.
What you'd revisit
the design deliberately does not scale one ACID primary is correct at 3 reservations/sec and is a single point of failure
for all booking. The Booking.com pivot means sharding on hotel_id plus a CDC-fed
inventory cache - and it introduces a cache/database inconsistency this design does
not currently have.
the pending timeout is an unpriced guess too short and a slow-but-successful payment gets its inventory released underneath
it, leaving a paid reservation with no room; too long and a failed checkout holds the
last room of a sold-out hotel for an hour. The right value depends on the PSP's
p99.9 latency, which nobody has measured.
overbooking is a flat 10% real revenue management sets it per hotel, per date, per room type from historical
cancellation rates - a resort in peak season cancels very differently from an airport
hotel on a Tuesday. A hard-coded multiplier is a placeholder for a model.
no group bookings '20 rooms for a wedding' spans multiple room types and may want all-or-nothing
semantics across them. The current UPDATE handles a date range for ONE room type.
the oversold-by-admin case has no the system correctly stops making it worse, and then a human has to relocate a guest.
workflow No tooling, no notification, no prioritisation of WHICH guest - which in practice is
where the actual product pain lives.
